doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Repertoire and the band's New York Dixieland style
summary: The band played four-beat Condon-influenced Dixieland with a bop drummer and banjo, seeing it as their own music.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: So were you playing the same kind of repertoire that the Alumni All-Stars play now?
I think we were a little more New York-Chicago based. I’m never happy with the labels very much.
Yes it’s hard to label things.

But I mean the real, as you can imagine, with Jimmy Wormworth on drums it was basically a bop drummer, we were a four beat Dixieland band, which is sort of interesting because we didn’t have a bass most of the time, we had a banjo. So it was kind of a unique mix to have the standard front line of trumpet, clarinet and trombone, but then sort of this mixed up rhythm section of a bop drummer, a really sort of classical or outstanding cocktail pianist piano player and a banjo player. But it worked fine. But I think we played much more — I can’t say swinging because I think the All-Stars swing now. But it was much more four beat and it was much more like Condon’s stuff. We were influenced very much in the fifties by what was going on in New York. Central Plaza, Nick’s, Condon’s.
So the group didn’t really think of itself as playing — I’m not sure how to put this — but old music.

That’s right. This was our music. You put it perfectly. This was our music. This was what was happening. I mean in those days New York City was the center of the world. I mean there was no other city that came close to it. And the jazz music was at New York City, was at Nick’s, the Central Plaza, and it was this kind of Dixieland. And of course all the great guys were playing then and we thought of that as, we did not think we were playing our father’s music.

But it was sort of interesting because we were and that was sort of one of the neat parts of it that we were playing this old stuff. I mean a tune like “Curse of an Aching Heart” is an old, old, old tune and yet you can make it swing like crazy and we did.
